content: Individuals with lymphatic filariasis (LF) may not experience difficulty in activities such as riding a bicycle unless they have large hydroceles, which can hinder such physical activities. Social stigma and limited access to services can significantly impact the social lives of individuals with lymphedema or elephantiasis, making it challenging for them to marry or secure suitable employment. Infection with adult worms or microfilariae is considered a form of impairment due to the associated lymphatic damage and compromised skin defenses. The progression of disability and participation restrictions resulting from these impairments highlights the importance of prevention strategies aimed at reducing their impact. The occurrence of LF is closely linked to living in endemic areas, poverty, social habits, and environmental factors. These infections lead to morbidity and can result in impairments and restrictions in daily life. The activities outlined in morbidity management and disability prevention (MMDP) programs address these restrictions through primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention measures. Primary prevention involves mass drug administration (MDA) to at-risk populations to reduce LF transmission and prevent new infections. Secondary and tertiary prevention focuses on providing care to infected individuals, with or without disabilities, in all areas with known patients, regardless of ongoing LF transmission. In 1997, the World Health Assembly resolved to eliminate LF as a public health problem. The World Health Organization (WHO) launched the Global Programme to Eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis (GPELF), which is based on two main components: halting LF transmission through MDA and alleviating suffering through morbidity management and disability prevention. MDA involves the annual administration of a combination of antifilarial drugs to entire at-risk populations. The treatment typically includes albendazole (400 mg), diethylcarbamazine (6 mg/kg) in areas without onchocerciasis or loiasis, and ivermectin (150–200 µg/kg). Alternative MDA regimens have been proposed to accelerate progress toward elimination goals. Drugs are administered for at least five years, the reproductive lifespan of adult worms. In areas with poor coverage or intense transmission, annual campaigns may need to be extended to ensure transmission interruption. MDA not only reduces transmission rates but also prevents the progression of subclinical to clinical disease and worsening morbidity. The benefits of MDA can be quantified in terms of the number of people protected and economic savings for health systems and individuals. Morbidity management and disability prevention are critical components of LF elimination. A significant portion of the public health burden of LF arises from impairments and disabilities related to lymphedema (or elephantiasis) and hydrocele. National programs must prioritize these activities to improve patient outcomes and enhance compliance with MDA. MMDP requires a comprehensive strategy involving secondary and tertiary prevention. Secondary prevention includes basic measures such as hygiene, skin and wound care, and elevation to prevent acute attacks and the progression of lymphedema to elephantiasis. Hydrocele management typically involves surgical intervention. Tertiary prevention includes psychological and socioeconomic support to ensure equal access to rehabilitation services and opportunities for health, education, and income. Beyond medical care, MMDP activities aim to combat stigma, promote positive attitudes toward individuals with disabilities, and support education, training, and income-generating initiatives. These efforts help individuals with LF fulfill their societal roles and overcome depression and economic losses associated with the disease. MMDP must continue in all areas with known patients, even after LF transmission has been interrupted, as chronically affected individuals are likely to remain in these communities. Integration of LF elimination into the control of other diseases is essential. GPELF is part of integrated efforts to prevent and treat neglected tropical diseases (NTDs), with collaboration across programs for preventive chemotherapy and vector control. WHO recommends an essential package of care to alleviate suffering in individuals with lymphedema and hydrocele. The measures for managing lymphedema can also be applied to other types of lymphedema detected in LF-endemic areas. Management of lymphedema could be integrated with care for other chronic diseases requiring long-term care, such as podoconiosis and diabetes. Essential care for LF patients aligns with an integrated skin NTD strategy, which includes leprosy, Buruli ulcer, podoconiosis, mycetoma, and other chronic skin diseases. It also complements care for conditions like diabetes, trauma, burns, obesity, venous insufficiency, and neurological diseases. Training healthcare workers, community members, and families to care for individuals with chronic disabling diseases is a key component of these programs. Hydrocele management complements initiatives to strengthen emergency and essential surgical care as part of universal health coverage (UHC). This includes enhancing surgical capacity at district hospitals and developing a sufficient health workforce to deliver necessary care. LF is a public health problem because the infection damages the lymphatic system, increasing the risk of secondary infections and complications. Managing morbidity and preventing disability are integral to achieving LF elimination as a public health problem. Access to care for lymphedema and hydrocele surgery can improve community cooperation in MDA campaigns, contributing to transmission interruption and prevention of new infections. The primary reason for managing morbidity is to relieve suffering, rooted in compassion. National programs must manage morbidity and prevent disability to eliminate LF, including care for affected individuals even after transmission interruption. Persons with clinical and social consequences of LF have a right to healthcare, and this responsibility lies with national elimination programs. UHC, a Sustainable Development Goal (SDG), ensures that all individuals and communities receive the health services they need without financial hardship. This can only be achieved if people at risk of or affected by NTDs have equitable access to high-quality health services. The GPELF target of 100% geographical coverage of essential care for LF patients aligns with UHC. Delivery of these services should be integrated with other quality health services and initiatives as appropriate. MMDP aims to provide every person with LF a better, more productive life and enable them to participate equally in the community, both socially and economically. By 2030, all national programs should achieve full geographical coverage of basic recommended care in all areas with known patients. The guiding principles for MMDP include access, flexibility, and integration of activities into other disease control programs. An essential package of care has been defined to address the main clinical manifestations of LF with established public health approaches. This package includes treating acute attacks, managing lymphedema, providing access to hydrocele surgery, and administering antifilarial medicines. Individuals with lymphedema must have access to lifelong care to manage the disease and prevent progression to advanced stages. MMDP should be part of the primary healthcare system to ensure sustainability.
